title: Hi, what's your name?
goal: Greet people at the right time of day, say your name, ask how someone is, and recognize the two ways of greeting: informal and formal.
bekal: greet with *ciao*, *buongiorno*, and *buonasera*, each at the right time
say your name and ask other people theirs
use *sono* and *sei* to say who you are

dialogs.title: Dialogo — Al primo giorno di corso
dialogs.intro: The first day of an Italian course in Bologna. Two new students sit down next to each other.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Ciao! Mi chiamo Budi. E tu?
lines.id: Hi! My name is Budi. And you?

lines.speaker: Giulia:
lines.id: I'm Giulia. Nice to meet you!

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Nice to meet you too. How are you?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: I'm fine too. Are you Italian?

lines.speaker: Giulia:
lines.text: Sì, sono di Bologna. E tu, sei cinese?
lines.id: Yes, I'm from Bologna. And you, are you Chinese?
lines.literal: yes, am of Bologna. and you, you-are Chinese?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: No, sono indonesiano. Sono di Giacarta.
lines.id: No, I'm Indonesian. I'm from Jakarta.
lines.literal: no, am Indonesian(male). am of Jakarta.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Thanks a lot! See you tomorrow, Giulia.

notes: **Ciao works both ways.** One word for both "hi" and "bye". Doubling it (*ciao ciao*) makes it sound light and warm — a typical casual goodbye.

**But ciao is informal.** With people you've just met who are clearly older, with officials, doctors, or your boss, Italian uses *buongiorno* (until about five in the afternoon) and *buonasera* (after that). Getting this wrong isn't a grammar mistake but a manners mistake — and people notice that more.

**Mi chiamo is not "my name is".** Literally it's "I call myself". That's why there is no word for "name" in it, and that's also why the question is *come ti chiami* — "how do you call yourself", not "what is your name".

**Io can be dropped.** *Io sono Giulia* and *Sono Giulia* are both correct. The verb form already tells you who the subject is, so the pronoun is only used for emphasis or contrast: *io sono di Bologna, tu sei di Giacarta*. That's the opposite of English, which always needs the subject.

**Come stai vs come sei.** Asking how someone is uses *stare*, not *essere*. *Come stai?* = how are you doing. *Come sei?* actually means "what are you like" — a question about personality, not well-being.

**Nationalities are lowercase.** *italiano*, *indonesiano*, *cinese* — unlike English. Country names keep their capital: *Italia*, *Indonesia*. The form also follows the speaker's gender: a man is *italiano*, a woman *italiana*.
**Anch'io** = "me too". The full form is *anche io*, but the two vowels in a row get clipped to *anch'io*. You'll see this kind of clipping often; Italian doesn't like two vowels colliding.

**Grazie mille** literally means "a thousand thanks". Italian exaggerates with numbers for emphasis, just like "thanks a million". The reply is *prego* — one all-purpose word meaning "you're welcome", "go ahead", and even "sorry, what was that?".

grammars.title: Essere — the verb "to be"
body: The first verb you have to master. It's irregular, so learn it as it is. In this unit you only need the first two rows; the rest follows in Unit 3.
after: Notice that *è* has an accent sloping to the left. Without the accent, *e* means "and" — the two words beginners mix up most: *lui e Giulia* (he and Giulia) is not at all *lui è Giulia* (he is Giulia).
The *io* and *loro* rows both happen to be *sono*. Context tells them apart, and in practice it's never confusing.

grammars.title: Greeting by the clock and by closeness
body: Two axes, not one. The first is time of day, the second is how close you are to the person you're talking to.
after: *Buonanotte* is not an ordinary evening greeting — it's what you say when parting to go to sleep. If you walk into a restaurant at eight in the evening and say it, you've just told everyone to go to bed.
*Salve* is a useful middle ground: more polite than *ciao*, more relaxed than *buongiorno*, and not tied to the clock. When in doubt, use this one.

sections.title: First words to keep in your pocket

blocks.text: The dozen or so words below cover most of the small talk on day one. Learn them whole; don't take the grammar apart yet.
*Scusa* for a friend, *scusi* for someone you address formally. This one-letter difference at the end will come up again and again throughout the course — it's the most common marker of politeness.

items: You walk into a bakery at eight in the morning. To the baker you say ____.
You meet a classmate on campus at ten. You say ____.
You walk into a restaurant at seven in the evening. To the waiter you say ____.
You part from your professor at the end of the hallway. You say ____.
You show a guest to their room at eleven at night. You say ____.

exercises.prompt: Put the words in the right order.

answers: Ciao! Come ti chiami? — Mi chiamo Budi. — Sono indonesiano. — Come stai? — Sto bene, grazie. — Sei di Bologna?
